title: Episodic records of deep microbial methanogenesis throughout the Caledonian mountain range exhumation
abstract:
Deep subsurface methanogenic life persists over extended geological timescales, showing resilience and reactivation across tectonic and thermal cycles, according to geochemical and geochronological analyses. 
 The deep continental biosphere hosts microbial communities employing ancient metabolisms such as methanogenesis. Yet, it is one of Earth’s least explored ecosystems with its long-term history remaining poorly constrained. This study integrated mineral, groundwater, and dissolved gas stable isotope analyses along with geochronological and previously published metagenomic data from the central Sweden 2276 m-deep COSC-2 borehole that intersects Silurian Caledonian thrust sheets and Precambrian basement. Extremely ¹³C-enriched fracture-filling calcite (δ¹³C up to + 28.9‰V-PDB) indicated ancient microbial methanogenesis down to 1907 m depth. U–Pb dating revealed multiple episodes of ¹³C-rich carbonate precipitation over hundreds of millions of years, including ages of 186 ± 20, 124 ± 20, 100 ± 22, 109 ± 17, 59 ± 4, and 1.8 ± 0.4 Ma along with a less certain age of 378 ± 65 Ma. Clumped-isotope temperatures decreased from ~70 to ~43 °C that reflected progressive exhumation. These results extend the temporal range of deep methanogenic biosignatures and demonstrate the resilience of subsurface life during long-term uplift and mountain range erosion. Deep subsurface methanogenic life persists over extended geological timescales, showing resilience and reactivation across tectonic and thermal cycles, according to geochemical and geochronological analyses.

title: Mounting damage and losses in the United States from post-wildfire flash floods and debris flows
abstract:
“Post-wildfire flash floods and debris flows are a mounting problem for people and the built environment, according to a 147-year inventory of damage and losses associated with the hazard in the United States.“ 
 Considerable progress has been made in forecasting the likelihood, magnitude, and mobility of post-wildfire flash floods and debris flows; however, we lack systematic observations of the physical and financial effects of these hazards, which can be used to close gaps between scientific understanding of the hazard and risk reduction. Here, we introduce a 147-year (1879–2025) inventory of damage and losses associated with post-fire flows in the United States. These observations enable an assessment of the geographic convergence and frequency of damaging post-fire flow events, as well as their multi-asset damage profiles and loss distributions. We find that the long-term (1879–2025) mean annual frequency of damaging flow events is greater than one and that recent (2016–2025) fatality rates and levels of monetary loss appear higher compared to historical periods. Our study provides an empirical baseline that can be used for long-term hazard planning amid global pressures compounded by wildland-urban interface expansion, increased wildfire activity, and rainfall intensification. “Post-wildfire flash floods and debris flows are a mounting problem for people and the built environment, according to a 147-year inventory of damage and losses associated with the hazard in the United States.“

title: Beyond direct ozone transport: Cross-regional transport of precursor pollutants intensifies ozone pollution over the Pearl River Delta
abstract:
•Transported precursor pollutants substantially enhance O3pollution in the PRD, yet local emission reductions can effectively offset this enhancement, highlighting the value of coupled local–regional mitigation strategies. •Transported OVOCs contribute 40–79% of the O3increase driven by transported VOCs and increase net O3production by up to 2.5 μg/m3/h, primarily in the central and southern PRD. •Transported APNs increase O3formation mainly in the eastern and northern PRD through the release of NOx, creating a spatially distinct enhancement pattern from that of OVOCs. 
 Cross-regional transport substantially influences ozone (O3) pollution over the Pearl River Delta (PRD) through the transport of both O3 and its precursors. Transported precursors can react with locally emitted precursors to produce O3, yet the detailed impacts of different precursor groups to O3 pollution remain poorly understood. Using the CAMx model, this study quantified the contributions of precursor transport to O3 pollution in the PRD during a severe multi-day episode in autumn 2018, which consisted of two periods: a cross-regional transport-dominated period (TRANS) and a stagnation period (STAG), driven by enhanced cross-regional transport and stagnation, respectively. Results indicate that daytime (10:00–18:00 local time) O3 and key precursors—particularly oxygenated volatile organic compounds (OVOCs) and acyl peroxy nitrates (APNs)—were notably modulated by cross-regional transport. While direct O3 transport contributed approximately 25-53% of surface O3 in the PRD, the contributions of precursor transport were considerable (13-21%), particularly transported VOCs and APNs as the primary drivers. OVOCs accounted for 40–79% of the transported VOCs contributions to O3 formation, followed by alkanes and alkenes. The resulting O3 concentration enhancements were mainly concentrated in the central and southwestern PRD, aligning with the distribution of VOC-limited regimes. The contributions of transported VOCs to O3 during the STAG period were higher than those during the TRANS period, especially in the central PRD. Under both the TRANS and STAG conditions, transported OVOCs accelerated net O3 production rates by up to 2.5 μg/m3/h in the central and southern PRD. In contrast, the impacts of transported APNs were confined to the eastern and northern PRD, where O3 production was mostly NOx-limited and NOx decomposed from APNs can efficiently enhance O3 production. Importantly, local emission reductions could partially counteract the O3 enhancement caused by these imported precursor pollutants, though the response was non-linear and depends on the local chemical regime and the magnitude of reductions. These findings therefore move beyond the conventional focus on direct O3 transport, revealing that imported OVOCs and APNs intensify O3 pollution through spatially distinct pathways. Effective O3 mitigation in receptor regions such as the PRD thus requires coupling stringent local controls with regionally coordinated emission reductions tailored to these contrasting precursor effects.
